title: New enemy and new tower in my synthetic slime mold tower defense game im working on.
author: Such--Balance
selftext:
Youre an alien slime mold taking over the world.

Humans will have none of it. Sending wave after wave of military personnel at you to stop your growth.

Suicide drones are especially nasty and will target weak points, potentially cutting of tendrils where your defenses are now sitting powerless once your slime mold has receded.

Regrow there once more to enable them again. At the price of valuable resources.

Also added the first of 6 new tower types all revolving around the purple alien tech this soon will have. The hover orb tower. Place it close to any border, and it will spawn a patrolling orb which will look for targets within range, border wide.

It takes time to traverse though, and will split firepower over more enemies if you have multiple of these towers. Cleverly design choke-points to get the most bang for your buck.

Working on this now for a couple of months. Still lots to be done. Lots.

I use ai for basically anything code wise. I dont have a team of bots all with different tasks like some do here. Usually i just add stuff in small steps, try to export tuneable parameters to fitting jsons and do all the finetuning there via old school human hand. Kinda like this more as a process too currently but that might just be because im pretty new to coding in general. So its nice to somewhat feel like im still learning and involved in all steps.

I did make some basic layers of enemy pathfinding which can all interact with eachother to create a somewhat diverse enemy intelligence which is reasonably easy to change based on those layers. Some can dodge tower ranges, some aim for weak territory tendrils, some path around walls and some will blast right through. I feel this can be optimized x10 still though by simplifying the base layers even further. Ups draw sometimes starts to be a slight problem with 100+ enemies all with varying behaviors. Couple that with the slime mold nature of the ever-changing territory which is also an added layer in the enemy pathfinding it can somewhat slow down with large numbers or lots of territory or towers. Tips more than welcome here to optimize further.

I do have a playable demo with 4 levels but no pressure. Not even close to be selling this yet, although its hella fun to create and play. Feedback is of course always more than welcome: [Synthetic System](https://twosecondgames.itch.io/synthetic-system)

I want to create something unique (if thats even possible these days) gameplay wise, and looks wise. Planning to go all out on the pixel puke nature of the alien territory look. It only got like 8 different shaders in it. Gotta pump those numbers up.

comments.author: ledniv
comments.body:
This looks really cool, and I actually like your workflow of keeping the tuneable values in JSON and doing the balancing by hand. That separation between designer data and runtime logic is useful even if AI is writing most of the code.

For the slowdown with 100+ enemies, I would profile before simplifying behavior. My first question would be whether every enemy is independently doing all of those pathfinding layers every frame. If so, that is probably where I would start. Keep enemy state in arrays, reference enemies by index, and maintain separate arrays for the enemies that actually need a new path, need to reconsider a target, need to avoid a tower, etc. Most enemies should be able to keep following their current result without recalculating everything every frame.

You can also look for navigation work that many enemies can share. If twenty enemies are moving through the same area toward the same territory, it is usually much cheaper to calculate useful navigation data for that area once and let all twenty consume it than to have twenty completely independent searches.

Since you are using AI for most of the code, I made a free Data Oriented Design skill for coding agents that teaches a lot of these rules around arrays, data locality, explicit state, and processing only the data that actually needs work:

[https://github.com/Data-Oriented-Design-for-Games/data-oriented-design](https://github.com/Data-Oriented-Design-for-Games/data-oriented-design)

Small plug: I cover the same ideas in much more depth in *High Performance Unity Game Development with Data Oriented Design*, including tool time data, arrays, branching, and organizing simulations so the CPU does less unnecessary work.

[https://www.manning.com/books/high-performance-unity-game-development](https://www.manning.com/books/high-performance-unity-game-development)
